More harm than good. That's my judgment, and here's the reasoning.

**The core argument is about counterfactuals.** The achievements usually credited to Mao — national reunification, expulsion of foreign domination, land redistribution, mass literacy, the collapse in infant mortality, the doubling of life expectancy from roughly 35 to the mid-60s — are real. But almost all of them were available to *any* competent modernizing Chinese government in that era. Taiwan and South Korea, starting from comparable poverty, achieved similar or better gains in literacy and life expectancy without killing tens of millions of their own people. Antibiotics, vaccination, and basic public health were transforming mortality across the entire developing world in those decades. China did somewhat better than average on health, largely through rural clinics and sanitation campaigns, and that deserves credit. It does not require Mao specifically.

The catastrophes, by contrast, were *distinctively his*. The Great Leap Forward famine — 30 million or more dead, the largest famine in recorded history — was not an unlucky harvest. It was the direct product of Mao's personal insistence on backyard steel, close planting, grain requisition quotas based on fabricated output figures, and his refusal to reverse course after Peng Dehuai told him the truth at Lushan in 1959. Peng was purged for saying it. The Cultural Revolution was likewise Mao's personal project, launched to destroy colleagues who had sidelined him after the famine, and it consumed a million-plus lives, shut the universities for years, and shattered China's scientific, cultural, and administrative capacity.

**The verdict follows from the asymmetry:** subtract Mao and keep the CCP, and you very plausibly get the unification, the land reform, the health and literacy gains, and faster industrial growth — without the two worst policy disasters of the twentieth century. That's roughly what happened after 1976, when Deng's reforms lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty using an institutional base that Mao had spent his last decade trying to wreck.

**The strongest case against me** is that Mao's leadership was genuinely decisive in the CCP's survival and victory between 1935 and 1949, and that without a unified state there is no platform for anything else. I take that seriously, and it's why I'd say the pre-1949 Mao and the post-1956 Mao should almost be assessed as different people. But a leader is judged on the whole record, and the twenty years he spent in unchallenged power after 1956 were overwhelmingly destructive. The CCP's own 1981 resolution conceded as much — "serious mistakes," "gross mistake," "grave disorder" — which is a remarkable admission from an institution that needs him as a founding myth.

A man who built a state and then repeatedly set it on fire out of ideological conviction and wounded pride has not, on balance, served his country well.

More harm than good. Here's why I think the evidence points that way.

**The core case against**

The Great Leap Forward famine of 1959–61 killed somewhere between 15 and 45 million people. Even the conservative estimates make it the deadliest famine in recorded history, and it was not a natural disaster. It was caused by forced collectivization, the abolition of private plots, absurd grain procurement quotas based on inflated local reports, the diversion of farm labor to backyard steel furnaces, and the continuation of grain exports while people starved. Mao was warned — most famously by Peng Dehuai at Lushan in 1959 — and responded by purging the messenger and intensifying the campaign. That sequence matters enormously for assigning responsibility.

The Cultural Revolution (1966–76) then consumed another decade. It killed on the order of one to two million people, destroyed China's universities for years, wrecked the civil service, sent intellectuals to the countryside, licensed factional violence that in places became civil war, and immiserated a generation. It was launched substantially to restore Mao's personal authority after the Leap had discredited him.

Add the earlier campaigns: land reform killings of perhaps one to two million "landlords," the Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries, the Anti-Rightist Campaign that destroyed roughly half a million careers after inviting criticism in the Hundred Flowers period.

**The honest case for**

It's real and shouldn't be dismissed. Mao's CCP unified a country that had been fragmented by warlords, invasion, and civil war for forty years. It ended foreign concessions and established genuine national sovereignty. Life expectancy roughly doubled, from the mid-30s to around 65 by 1976. Literacy rose dramatically. The 1950 Marriage Law, banning arranged marriage and concubinage and permitting divorce, was a genuine emancipation for hundreds of millions of women. Mass public health campaigns and the "barefoot doctor" system extended basic medicine into villages that had never had any. An industrial base was built from nearly nothing. Amartya Sen's comparison is worth taking seriously: India's chronic deprivation may have produced more cumulative excess deaths over the same decades than China's acute famine.

**Why the case for doesn't carry**

The decisive question isn't "was 1976 China better than 1949 China" — almost any government would have improved on 1949, which was the nadir of a century of collapse. The question is what Mao specifically added and subtracted relative to the plausible alternatives.

And when you separate Mao from the Chinese Communist Party, the ledger separates too. The achievements — unification, land redistribution, public health, literacy, women's legal status — were products of a disciplined party-state carrying out programs that the broader leadership supported and that other developing states were also achieving in the same decades. The catastrophes were distinctively Mao's, pushed through over the objections of colleagues like Peng, Liu Shaoqi, Chen Yun, and Deng Xiaoping. The 1962–65 recovery, run largely by Liu and Deng while Mao was sidelined, worked. That's the natural experiment: when the party governed without Mao driving it, outcomes improved; when Mao reasserted control, he produced the Cultural Revolution.

The life-expectancy argument is the strongest pro-Mao point, but it cuts both ways: the gains came mostly from cheap, basic interventions — sanitation, vaccination, famine-free years, elementary clinics — and the single largest interruption to that trend was Mao's own famine, which caused life expectancy to crater to around 30 in 1960. Taiwan and South Korea, starting from comparably poor positions, achieved better health and vastly better growth without killing tens of millions.

Even the CCP's own 1981 verdict — "70 percent good, 30 percent bad" — was a political compromise necessary to preserve the party's legitimacy, and it still called the Cultural Revolution a decade of catastrophe. That is a remarkable thing for a regime to say about its own founder, and it suggests the real ratio is worse than the official one.

My verdict: Mao was essential to the founding of modern China and then became the principal obstacle to its development. The founding could have had other authors. The famine and the Cultural Revolution could not.

**More harm than good.** The verdict rests less on tallying achievements against atrocities than on a single question: which of Mao's effects were actually attributable to *him*, as opposed to being achievable by almost any competent modernizing government China might have had?

The achievements credited to him are real. The People's Republic ended a century of fragmentation, warlordism, and foreign predation, and restored China as a sovereign actor. Life expectancy roughly doubled between 1949 and 1976, from the high thirties to the mid-sixties. Literacy went from perhaps 20 percent to around two-thirds. Land was taken from landlords and given to peasants. The 1950 Marriage Law, the abolition of footbinding, and the movement of women into paid work were genuine social revolutions. Amartya Sen's argument is sound: the human-capital base built in these years is part of why China outran India after 1979.

But nearly all of that was being accomplished elsewhere in East Asia at the same time, with far less blood. Taiwan carried out a thoroughgoing land reform, raised literacy and life expectancy on a comparable trajectory, and built an industrial base — under an authoritarian government that was itself brutal, yet killed on a scale orders of magnitude smaller. South Korea did much the same. Mass vaccination, basic sanitation, and antibiotics were lifting mortality across the developing world in those decades. The gains were the common property of the era's developmental states; they were not Mao's signature.

What *was* Mao's signature — the things that happened because he specifically held power and overrode his colleagues — was ruinous. The Great Leap Forward produced the largest famine in human history, with credible estimates of excess deaths ranging from 15 to 45 million and most serious scholarship clustering around 30 million. This was not a natural disaster. It followed from backyard steel furnaces that destroyed tools and diverted labor, from communal kitchens, from fantastical procurement quotas set on the basis of falsified harvest reports, and above all from a political atmosphere — established by the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign and sealed by Peng Dehuai's purge at Lushan in 1959 — in which telling Mao the truth was a career-ending or life-ending act. Grain continued to be exported while peasants ate seed stock and bark.

The Cultural Revolution was a second self-inflicted wound: on the order of a million to two million dead, tens of millions persecuted, universities closed for years, scientific and administrative institutions gutted, a generation's education sacrificed, and a culture of denunciation that reached into families. Its purpose was not development. Its purpose was Mao's recovery of personal supremacy after the Leap discredited him. Add the earlier campaigns — the suppression of counterrevolutionaries, the land reform killings, the half-million intellectuals labeled rightists — and the toll from deliberate policy exceeds that of most wars.

There is also an opportunity cost that rarely gets counted. China's per capita output grew slowly and erratically under Mao while its neighbors compounded. Consumption per head in the countryside in 1976 was close to what it had been in the mid-1950s. The reforms after 1978 worked in large part by dismantling his agricultural and industrial model, which is an implicit verdict rendered by the Party itself.

The strongest reply is that unification and the construction of a capable state were preconditions for everything that followed, and that only a movement with Mao's ruthlessness could have achieved them. I don't find this persuasive. The CCP's victory in 1949 was a collective achievement with many architects, and the regime's most productive years — 1949 to 1957, and again 1962 to 1965 — were precisely the periods when Mao's personal direction was weakest and pragmatists like Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, and Deng Xiaoping were running things. The evidence suggests the Party could have built a modern state without the Leap and the Cultural Revolution. Mao is the reason it didn't.

He unified a country and then spent two decades wrecking it. The Party's own formula of "seventy percent right, thirty percent wrong" is a political settlement, not a historical finding. The honest ledger runs the other way.

**No. On balance, over the full 65 years, the Revolution did not make life better for most Cubans — though it did make it better for some Cubans, especially in its first two decades.**

Here's why I land there.

**The genuine gains were real, and I won't minimize them.** Pre-1959 Cuba was relatively prosperous by Latin American standards but brutally unequal between Havana and the countryside. Rural Cubans faced seasonal unemployment in the sugar "dead season," low literacy, and almost no medical access. The 1961 literacy campaign, the expansion of rural clinics, land reform, and the dismantling of legal racial segregation delivered concrete improvements to millions of people who had been left out. Infant mortality fell from roughly 35 per 1,000 to among the lowest in the hemisphere. Cuba also avoided the death-squad slaughters that consumed Guatemala, El Salvador, Argentina, and Chile in the same decades — a real achievement that comparisons often skip.

**But the gains were not sustainable, and that matters enormously.** The welfare state of the 1970s and 80s was underwritten by Soviet subsidies estimated at a quarter or more of Cuban GDP. When they vanished in 1991, the "Special Period" cut GDP by about a third, drove average caloric intake below 1,900 a day, and produced an epidemic of optic neuropathy affecting tens of thousands from malnutrition. A development model that collapses the moment a foreign patron disappears was never really a development model. Today Cuba endures daily blackouts, acute food and medicine shortages, and crumbling housing — not as a historical aberration but as the recurring condition.

**The relative decline is damning.** Cuba entered 1959 near the top of Latin America in income and health indicators and is now near the bottom in income. The Dominican Republic, poorer and less literate than Cuba in 1959, now has substantially higher living standards. Costa Rica achieved comparable health and education outcomes — Cuba's signature accomplishments — while remaining democratic and several times richer. The embargo imposed real costs, and I don't dismiss them; but Cuba has traded freely with Canada, Europe, Latin America, and Asia for decades. The embargo explains some of the shortfall, not the structural failure of a centrally planned economy that couldn't feed an island with good soil.

**The political cost was not incidental — it was the mechanism of the failure.** Cubans got free schooling but no free press, no independent unions, no opposition parties, no way to vote out a government whose policies were impoverishing them. Thousands were imprisoned for political offenses; gay men, Jehovah's Witnesses, and dissidents were sent to UMAP labor camps in the 1960s; the 2021 protests ended in hundreds of convictions. This isn't just a moral debit to set against a material credit. The absence of accountability is *why* catastrophic policies — the 1970 ten-million-ton sugar harvest, the perpetual dependence on a single patron, the refusal to reform after 1991 — went uncorrected for decades.

**The clearest verdict is the one Cubans have rendered themselves.** Roughly 1.5 to 2 million left between 1959 and 2020. Since 2021, over a million more have gone — close to a tenth of the population in four years, the largest exodus in Cuban history, including the young, the educated, and the doctors and teachers the system produced. Thousands have died on rafts in the Straits. People do not abandon a country at that rate, at that risk, if the project is delivering.

**The fair summary:** the Revolution redistributed dignity and basic services to a rural and Black underclass that the old order had abandoned, and for a generation that was a genuine improvement in their lives. But it financed those gains on borrowed geopolitical time, destroyed the economy's capacity to sustain them, and stripped Cubans of any lawful means to change direction. A Cuban born in 1960 may have gotten a better childhood than their parents. A Cuban born in 1990 got rationing, blackouts, and a one-way flight. That is not a better life — it is a promise made to one generation and defaulted on for the next.
